The subscriber is only picked up again once the 60-minute claim goes stale, so this partly brings back symptom 1 (silent loss).

v.rationale:
I ran the full test suite for all four implementations and every one passes. I then ran a shared set of throwaway probes against each: 1500-row dispatch, outage then recovery through the database queue, the 'Queued N' count on a repeat run, and job behaviour while the per-subscriber overlap lock is held. All probe files have been deleted.

Each implementation fixed bug 4 (chunk → chunkById), bug 3 (a bounded withoutOverlapping expiry) and bug 1 (letting the exception reach the worker). They differ on bug 2 and on how robust the job is.

impl-2 ranks first. Its atomic claim plus lazyById dispatched all 1500 rows. With releaseAfter, MaxExceptions and 10 tries, a held lock delays the job rather than failing or deleting it, and it uses the modern queue attributes. Its weaknesses are a redundant second dedupe layer (the claim plus ShouldBeUnique) and an attribute-reflection test.

impl-1 ranks second. It has the same solid atomic-claim design, but dontRelease() silently deleted the job in my probe (no row in jobs or failed_jobs), which partly brings back the 'never reaches the CRM' symptom until the 60-minute claim goes stale. It also uses older property-style configuration.

impl-4 ranks third. It never fixed the dispatcher itself. It hides the duplicate problem behind ShouldBeUnique, so the dispatcher still rewrites every unsynced row each minute and reports false 'Queued N' counts, and its failed() reset of crm_sync_queued_at has no effect. It does have the best end-to-end recovery test.

impl-3 ranks last. Its dispatcher brings back the exact offset-chunk-while-mutating bug it fixed in the normalize command; only 1000 of 1500 rows were queued per run. Its overlap middleware has no release delay and only 3 tries, so in my probe a held lock sent the job to failed_jobs without ever calling the CRM.
